summary: Polaris AI and Redwood discussed options for BYOK, HSM integration, cross-border key custody, and encryption both at-rest and in-transit. Key topics: envelope encryption, key wrapping, KMIP/HSM connectivity, audit log retention, SOC 2/ISO evidence, SSO/RBAC gating for key ops. Agreed next steps: share checklist, schedule HSM vendor call, and provide audit/log samples.
topics: data residency and cross-border key handling
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining — we have about 50 minutes. Quick intro, I'm Maya, AE, and with me is Diego from SE.
[00:10] Aisha Rahman: Hi all, Aisha here. We're kicking off a security review focused on encryption and key custody for our generative stack.
[00:18] Diego Alvarez: Great, thanks Aisha. Tom, Mei — thanks for being here. Can you share a little about your current key setup? Are you already using a cloud KMS or an on-prem HSM?
[00:28] Tom Becker: We're using a managed KMS for most workloads, but for models that touch customer PII we want customer-held keys. So BYOK is critical. We also have a hardware security module in our co-lo for legacy apps.
[00:40] Mei Lin: From compliance side we need audit trails 7 years for certain EU contracts and evidence for SOC 2 and ISO. We also want RBAC such that only a small ops group can rotate keys.
[00:52] Diego Alvarez: Understood. Redwood supports BYOK with two common patterns: (1) cloud KMS customer-owned keys (we integrate via IAM + key policies), and (2) bring your own HSM — either cloud HSM or on-prem via KMIP/PKCS#11 gateway. We do envelope encryption by default — model artefacts encrypted with a data key, wrapped by your customer key. That keeps rekey cheap and auditable.
[01:12] Tom Becker: Envelope — ok, that matches what we do. But what about cross-border concerns? Some of our inference instances spin up in EU regions and keys cannot leave EU for certain customers.
[01:22] Diego Alvarez: We can pin key usage to region. Two options: keep the customer key in an EU-resident KMS/HSM and route EU traffic to EU hosts; or use a geo-sharded key replication architecture where wrapped keys travel but primary key material never leaves region. There are tradeoffs with latency and failover.
[01:38] Aisha Rahman: If we pin to EU HSMs, how do you handle failover? Suppose EU region goes down — do you failover to US with a copy of the key? That would break residency.
[01:46] Diego Alvarez: Correct, an automatic failover that moves primary key material would violate residency. We recommend explicit runbook-based failover: in an outage, you could manual-authorize temporary cross-region use, with audit and governance controls. We can support policy flags to prevent automatic cross-border key use.
[02:04] Mei Lin: Good. About HSM connectivity — our vendor uses KMIP. Is that supported out of the box?
[02:10] Maya Chen: Yes, we support KMIP for HSMs and PKCS#11 for some appliances; for cloud HSMs we use provider-specific connectors. Diego has a vendor integration checklist we can share.
[02:19] Diego Alvarez: Right. The integration usually involves: network VPN or private peering, mutual TLS, KMIP over TLS, and strict firewall rules. We also recommend a jumpbox for management plane traffic and key rotation ops.
[02:30] Tom Becker: What about key rotation windows — our policy is 90 days for symmetric keys on customer-facing endpoints. Will that cause re-encryption headaches for models?
[02:38] Diego Alvarez: Envelope encryption mitigates that — rotating the master wrapping key does not require re-encrypting all model blobs; you re-wrap the data keys. We can support rolling rotation with zero-downtime if you use the rotation workflow in our docs. We'll provide a sample rotation script.
[02:51] Aisha Rahman: Audit logs — we need proof of key access and rotation events forwarded to our SIEM. Can Redwood stream audit events to our collector?
[02:59] Diego Alvarez: Yes, we emit fine-grained audit events: key usage, wrap/unwrap ops, KMS errors, and admin changes. We support pushing via syslog, Kafka topic, or API webhook. For retention, default is 90 days; extended retention is available as an add-on for 7 years.
[03:17] Mei Lin: Is the audit trail tamper-evident? We need chain-of-custody evidence.
[03:21] Diego Alvarez: We provide signed audit bundles for compliance windows — log entries are appended with cryptographic signatures and a monotonically increasing sequence ID. For stronger guarantees you can pump logs into your own WORM storage.
[03:34] Tom Becker: Who can perform key revocation or deletion? We need RBAC such that deletion requires multi-person approval.
[03:40] Maya Chen: Redwood's control plane integrates with your SSO (SAML/SCIM) and maps AD groups to roles. You can require MFA, and for destructive ops we support an approver workflow: n-out-of-m signature or manual approval ticketing integration.
[03:55] Aisha Rahman: Sounds good. A couple of nitty-gritty questions: encryption in transit between the model runtime and the KMS — is it mutual TLS? What ciphers?
[04:03] Diego Alvarez: We use mTLS with TLS 1.3 by default, with AES-GCM suites. For KMIP we run KMIP over TLS; for PKCS#11 we prefer an IPsec/VPN tunnel or private link.
[04:13] Mei Lin: Any FIPS-140 requirements? Some of our customers require FIPS-validated modules.
[04:17] Diego Alvarez: We can integrate with FIPS-validated HSMs; our stack is compatible with FIPS modules provided by your vendor for the KMS. We can provide compatibility notes per vendor.
[04:27] Tom Becker: Regarding encryption at rest for model weights and KV caches — are those encrypted with the same data keys or separate keys per tenant?
[04:35] Diego Alvarez: We recommend per-tenant data keys generated from a tenant-specific master key; keys are namespaced per account. This provides crypto multitenancy isolation and simpler rotation without cross-tenant impact.
[04:47] Aisha Rahman: If an attacker compromises a control-plane credential, can they unwrap keys?
[04:51] Diego Alvarez: Control-plane credentials alone are insufficient. Key unwrapping requires an auditable operation that also checks RBAC and SSO context; we log the requestor identity and source IP. For extra defense in depth you can enable HSM-enforced policies disallowing unwraps from management plane tokens.
[05:05] Mei Lin: What about secrets storage for service-to-service auth between Redwood runtime and KMS — do you store client certs?
[05:11] Diego Alvarez: Service certs are rotated automatically and stored in our secrets manager; but for BYOK we recommend you host the private key material in your HSM. For client auth we do mutual cert exchange and short-lived tokens.
[05:24] Tom Becker: Any hard limits or throughput constraints if we route a large inference volume against an external HSM?
[05:30] Diego Alvarez: External HSMs can become a bottleneck if every token causes a RMK unwrap. That's why we use caching of unwrapped data keys (KV cache) at the runtime with strict TTL and reuse policies to reduce HSM calls. We also recommend batching key operations and pre-warming key cache. We'll share best-practice config values.
[05:50] Aisha Rahman: We also want to avoid key material transit over public internet.
[05:54] Diego Alvarez: All KMS traffic can go via private peering or VPN; we do not require traffic to traverse the internet for KMIP connections if you set up private connectivity.
[06:02] Mei Lin: For evidence, can you share samples of the signed audit bundle and schema?
[06:07] Diego Alvarez: Yes, Diego: I'll attach a sample bundle and the event schema after the call.
[06:12] Maya Chen: We'll also drop our BYOK onboarding checklist and the HSM integration worksheet. Link: <redwood.link/byok-checklist> (placeholder).
[06:21] Tom Becker: One more — key import: do you support key wrapping/import with wrapped key material or direct key injection? Some HSMs require wrapped import keys.
[06:30] Diego Alvarez: We support wrapped key import flows and direct import via KMIP depending on vendor. We also support key attestation where the HSM provides proof of key generation origin.
[06:40] Mei Lin: Compliance question — for SOC 2 we need time-stamped evidence of key rotation, and for ISO we need change control records. Do your logs include correlative request IDs for change tickets?
[06:49] Diego Alvarez: Yes, logs include user, ticket ID (if provided), request ID, and before/after key metadata. We can optionally include JIRA/CI/CD link fields in the audit record.
[06:58] Aisha Rahman: Anything else on encryption in transit — what about east-west between inferencing nodes?
[07:04] Diego Alvarez: East-west is encrypted in our runtime via mTLS and intra-cluster encryption; we can enable strict network policies and require mutual auth.
[07:10] Tom Becker: OK, let's talk timeline. We want a pilot with BYOK and EU-residency for a subset of customers by end of Q2.
[07:18] Maya Chen: That's doable. Proposed plan: week 1 onboarding checklist and network prep; week 2 HSM connectivity test; week 3 pilot run with audit sampling.
[07:26] Mei Lin: We'll need to review the legal annex for key custody too.
[07:29] Maya Chen: We'll share the draft annex and propose redlines.
[07:33] (short crosstalk)
[07:36] Diego Alvarez: Quick note — one common pitfall: caching too-long TTL for unwrapped keys. It simplifies latency but raises blast radius. We'll include recommended TTLs for different SLOs.
[07:47] Aisha Rahman: Thanks, this was helpful.
[07:49] Maya Chen: Recap: we'll send BYOK checklist, audit schema, and schedule HSM vendor session. Any other immediate asks?
[07:56] Tom Becker: Please include a sample runbook for cross-border emergency failover.
[08:00] Maya Chen: Noted.
[08:02] Mei Lin: Thank you.
[08:03] Maya Chen: Great — we'll follow up with the artifacts and follow-up meeting invite. Bye all.
[08:06] (call end)
notes: Polaris requires EU residency for certain customers; no automatic cross-region key failover without manual approval.
Redwood to provide BYOK checklist and HSM vendor integration worksheet.
Audit retention default 90 days; extended retention add-on available for 7 years (compliance add-on).
